analysis.one_liner: Lets federal regulators require water testing and chemical disclosure for fracking on public lands.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in two House subcommittees for two years and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Mineral Leasing Act so the Bureau of Land Management must regulate hydraulic fracturing on federal lands. It would require companies to test water before drilling and publicly disclose the chemicals they inject underground. It would also remove a loophole that currently exempts fracking fluids from the Safe Drinking Water Act's underground injection rules, putting them under the same drinking-water protections as other underground waste injection.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near or use lands and water downstream of federal oil and gas leases. Baseline water testing would establish who caused contamination before drilling starts, and public chemical disclosure would let residents and doctors know what is in the fluids injected near aquifers. Communities whose drinking water comes from wells near federal leases would gain the most.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rural residents near federal drilling leases

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Bureau of Land Management to regulate hydraulic fracturing operations on federal lands, with baseline water testing and public internet disclosure of the chemicals used as conditions of every permit [S3].

Removes fracking fluids from the Safe Drinking Water Act's underground-injection exemption, so those fluids would fall under state underground injection control programs that protect drinking water [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies operating on federal lands would bear the cost of water testing, chemical disclosure, and federal permits. Some operators might delay or forgo drilling where those costs are significant. Companies could also lose some ability to keep their chemical mixtures confidential.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies on federal lands

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts acidizing and other well-stimulation techniques from its definition of hydraulic fracturing, so companies could shift to chemically similar methods that avoid the testing and disclosure requirements [S3].

Federal permitting requirements could slow development on federal lands, which would reduce lease revenue that funds public services in western states and could raise production costs relative to drilling on private land [S2].

Industry groups have long argued federal fracking rules duplicate state regulation; the bill does not address how federal standards would interact with state permitting programs outside the drinking-water rules [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections are modest and targeted: a water test before drilling and telling the public what chemicals are being injected next to drinking water sources. The cost falls on a specific industry on public lands, not on the general public. The main design weakness is the acidizing exemption, which leaves a real escape hatch for operators who want to avoid disclosure.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees, then parked in subcommittees on environment and on energy and mineral resources, and no committee ever acted on it before the two-year Congress expired.

narrative.text: Represent Darren Soto introduced the bill on January 10, 2019, and it was referred to the Natural Resources and Energy and Commerce Committees [S5].
No member cosponsored it; the cosponsor list stayed at zero for the entire Congress [S4].

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change on January 25, 2019 and to the Natural Resources Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on February 5, 2019, where it remained without a markup, hearing, or floor vote through the end of the Congress [S5].
The 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021, so the bill expired without any recorded vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas operators on federal lands are better off: for two more years no federal water-testing, chemical-disclosure, or permit conditions were layered onto their operations, and they remain free to use fracking fluids without Safe Drinking Water Act underground-injection oversight.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas operators on federal lands

for.name: Rep. Darren Soto

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in January 2019; found no cosponsors and no committee took it up.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill in either committee during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Major lessee of federal lands affected by federal fracking rules
against.what_they_did: No recorded activity on this specific bill; the industry broadly opposed federal fracking permitting rules of this kind during the period.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no members signed on besides the Democratic sponsor, so the partisan split on the bill itself was never tested; Democrats held the House majority during this period and the bill sat entirely within their committees' control.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies operating on federal lands
industries.note: The bill would require baseline water testing, public chemical disclosure, and BLM permits for every fracking operation on federal land, adding direct compliance costs and ending the current exemption of fracking fluids from Safe Drinking Water Act underground injection rules. Because these operations inject fluids next to aquifers that residents draw on, the industry's interest in avoiding these requirements runs against nearby residents' interest in clean water.

industries.industry: Federal land water users and nearby rural communities
industries.note: Not an industry, but the concentrated beneficiary: public water testing and chemical disclosure would give residents and local health officials the information to trace contamination to a specific operator.
